narrative: Star Vetter automatically identifies eclipsing binary star systems in data from NASA's TESS satellite. An eclipsing binary is a pair of stars orbiting each other such that, from Earth's viewpoint, one star regularly passes in front of the other, causing the light we receive to dim in a predictable pattern. This project samples targets from TESS observations, measures their light curves, applies statistical tests to separate real eclipsing binaries from false signals, and cross-checks each candidate against six major variable-star catalogs to avoid re-reporting known systems. Candidates that pass all statistical gates and show no catalog match proceed to a fully automated pixel-level check that examines whether the light-curve signal is truly coming from the intended target. We confirm 321 candidates so far from a sample covering 2.6% of the TESS survey footprint. Each confirmed candidate is listed here with its measured orbital period and eclipse depths, along with any open caveats noted during the vetting process.

faqs.question: What is an eclipsing binary?
faqs.answer: An eclipsing binary is a pair of stars orbiting each other in such an orientation that, as seen from Earth, one star regularly passes in front of the other. When this happens, the combined light we receive dims. By measuring this dimming pattern over time - called a light curve - we can infer the orbital period (how long one complete cycle takes) and the relative depths of the eclipses, which depend on the sizes and temperatures of the two stars.

faqs.question: What do 'candidate' and 'confirmed' mean on this site?
faqs.answer: 'Candidate' refers to any target that shows statistical signs of being an eclipsing binary but has not yet passed the pixel-level check. 'Confirmed' means the candidate has passed an automated pixel-level examination that verifies the light-curve signal is coming from the intended target and not from a nearby star or other contaminant. Confirmation here means the signal is real and on-target; it does not imply any broader scientific verification or that the system has been studied by other researchers.

faqs.question: What is the machine learning screening score?
faqs.answer: Star Vetter includes a machine learning model (gradient boosting) trained on 3265 labeled examples to provide a second opinion on candidate quality. This model outperforms the current rule-based pipeline. However, it is used only for ranking or comparison; it does not currently gate, filter, or decide which candidates receive the pixel-level check. The pipeline's vetting decisions are made by rule-based statistical tests and catalog cross-matching.

faqs.question: How does a candidate get checked?
faqs.answer: Every candidate that passes statistical vetting gates and shows no match in six major variable-star catalogs automatically proceeds to a pixel-level check. This check is fully automated and examines whether the eclipse signal is truly centered on the target star or arises from a nearby star or other source. Candidates that pass this check are confirmed and listed on this site.

faqs.question: What if the period looks like an alias?
faqs.answer: The pipeline tests for period aliases - cases where the true period might be half (or twice) the measured period - by comparing the eclipse depths of odd-numbered cycles against even-numbered cycles. If the depths differ significantly, it suggests the period measurement may be aliased. Such candidates are flagged on their individual pages so users are aware of this caveat.

faqs.question: Can I verify a result myself?
faqs.answer: Yes. Every confirmed candidate links to its TESS light curve in the Mikulski Archive for Space Telescopes (MAST). You can download the data and examine the eclipse pattern yourself. The orbital period and measured eclipse depths are listed to help guide your inspection.

faqs.question: What happens to a candidate after it is listed here?
faqs.answer: Being listed on Star Vetter is the end of this automated pipeline's work. The site itself does not perform follow-up observations, add candidates to official catalogs, or coordinate further study. Whether a confirmed candidate receives attention from the broader research community is beyond the scope of this project.
